corrected_value.authors: Clark, C. J., Luguri, J. B., Ditto, P. H., Knobe, J., Shariff, A. F., & Baumeister, R. F.
corrected_value.title: Free to punish: A motivated account of free will belief.

decisions.quote:
Clark, C. J., Luguri, J. B., Ditto, P. H., Knobe, J., Shariff, A. F., & Baumeister, R. F. (2014). Free to punish: A
         motivated account of free will belief. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 106, 501–513.
         doi:10.1037/a0035880
decisions.reason: Studies 1, 2a, and 2b directly replicate Studies 1 and 2 of Clark et al. (2014), quoting pages 502-511 of the published Journal of Personality and Social Psychology article and listing its DOI (10.1037/a0035880) in the reference list. The shipped record used a conflicting PsycEXTRA conference abstract DOI (10.1037/e578192014-061), which the codebook rules out in favor of the cited published article.

decisions.quote:
Across replication experiments we found no evidence for the original claim that
witnessing immoral behavior causes people to increase their belief in free will, though we did
replicate the finding that people attribute more free will to agents who behave immorally
compared to a neutral control (Studies 2a & 3).
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind codings correctly record a mixed outcome for Clark et al. (2014). The authors report failing to replicate the original finding that exposure to immoral behavior increases general free will beliefs (Studies 1, 2a, and 2b) or that desire to punish mediates general free will beliefs, while replicating the original finding that people attribute more agent-specific free will to immoral agents relative to a neutral control (Studies 2a and 3, with punishment mediating agent-specific attributions in Studies 2a and 2b).

decisions.quote:
Studies 1 and 2b are exact replications of Clark et
al.’s (2014) Studies 1 and 2, respectively, and our Study 2a is a close replication of Clark et al.
(2014) Study 2 (we use identical measures and procedures, but a different sample population). In
these experiments we seek to replicate the finding that people inflate their belief in free will after
being exposed to another agent’s immoral behavior and that the desire to punish immoral actors
mediates the relationship between behavior and people’s belief in free will.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind codings correctly classify the record as a replication because the paper collects new experimental data across independent participant samples (Studies 1, 2a, 2b, and 3) to re-test the published findings of Clark et al. (2014).
